Hello, this is a message for the students of the international trade group. I am recording it on Sunday evening, because a few things are changing this week. First, Professor Lindqvist is traveling, so Tuesday's seminar is moving to Thursday, at the same time. Second, we are still waiting for four thesis proposals. If you are working on yours right now, do not worry about the length. Send me the two pages you have and we will talk. Third, the library is closing early all week, because they are installing new equipment on the second floor. And one last thing. Two of you are asking me the same question about the reading list, so I am putting the answer in writing tomorrow morning. Please read that email before you write to me again. Thank you.

Right now, while we are talking, about two hundred ships are waiting outside Brazilian ports, and most of them are carrying corn or soybeans. That number is going up every week at this time of year, and it tells you more about the market than any price on a screen does. Here is why. A trader is not only buying a product. He is buying a date. If a ship is sitting outside Santos for eleven days instead of three, somebody is paying for those eight days, and the contract decides who. So when people ask me what is happening in the grain market this month, I never start with the price. I start with the queue. The queue is the market talking, and at the moment it is saying that everybody is in a hurry.
